For Foreign Travellers FORMALITIES : As prevalent in the North Eastern Sector, foreign tourists intending to visit Meghalaya require Restricted Area Permits. The applications stating complete details of name, passport number (its issuing authority and the expiry date), place of birth, profession, duration of stay and the

purpose of visit, should be addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, North Block, New Delhi 110001, well in advance of undertaking the trip. However, the Foreigners' Regional Registration Officers of the Government of India at New Delhi, Bombay, Calcutta and Madras are authorised to grant Restricted Area Permits to organised groups of foreign tourists. This, however, is subject to the condition that the visits are confined strictly to Shillong, Cherrapunjee, Barapani, Mawsynram, Jakrem, Ranikor, Thadlaskein, Nartiang, Tura & Slju. Permitted foreign tourists have to travel to Guwahati and back by air and then travel by a prescribed route to these places. They have to visit in groups, minimum of four members, their duration of stay cannot exceed ten days and visits are to be organised only by recognised travel agencies. DO'S AND DON'TS Photography at airports is prohibited. Foreign nationals can pay their hotel bills in foreign cuuency, in Indian Rupees or by travellers cheques. Exchange your money only through authorised banks/money changers, or you may find yourself with counterfeit money. Insist on a receipt when exchanging your money. Retain all exchange receipts with you as without them, you cannot reconvert your unspent money on your final departure from India. Export of most wildlife and their products is banned or strictly regulated. Insist on getting a certificate for the legitimate purchase of

articles made of a particular animal product and permission for its export. Export of antiques over 100 years old is prohibited. While shopping, avoid touts and brokers. It UVE VIBRANT EXCITING New Frontier Colour Lab (P) Ltd. Regd. Office and Lab : S.S. Road. Lakhtokia, (iuwahati 1 Phone : 34686, 544011 Travel Tips Shillong is cosmopolitan in nature. Local customs and etiquette have been dealt with seperately in this book. Living conditions range from star-category hotels to budget ones. Tourist Bungalow and Youth Hostel facilities are also available. It is advisable to make travel arrangements in advance especially if you are planning to travel within September to May (the high tourist season). Do include one or two more destinations in your itinerary, say Guwahati and Kaziranga, so as to get a real taste of the North East. Try to fit in a fair or festival and let your senses exhilarate to the colours and gaiety. English is understood and spoken in Meghalaya. Assamese, Bengali, Hindi and Nepali are also spoken. We have devoted some space to the usage of Khasi which is the local language. Meghalayans are hospitable and friendly people, never need a tourist be lost on the streets. Someone will always help you reach

your destination. Professional help is readily available from the Govt, of India and Meghalaya Tourism staff. It is always advisable to carry packed lunch and bottled drinks when setting out for the day. ('Avomine 1 tablets are definite help for those suffering from travel sickness.) If you have a weak stomach, stick to mineral water, bottled drinks, coffee, tea, beer or wine during meals. Tap water is not always chlorinated. In case you fall sick, Shillong has excellent doctors, chemists and hospitals. Ask your hotel to recommend a doctor if you ever need one. Always remember to pack an umbrella - rains are a normal day-do-day matter. Bring your camera and colour films by all means. Meghalaya has a lot to offer to the nature lover. Colour films and processing facilities are easily available at Shillong. It is safe to travel within Meghalaya. Even if you read of some trouble at times, do not be discouraged, as these are stray incidents. Credit Cards are accepted by hotels, travel agents, shops and restaurants. 10% tipping is customary in case your hotel bills do not include service charges. This would come down to 5% if you are travelling with a group. Taxis in Shillong do not run on meters. Take help of your hotel receptionist and settle the taxi fare in advance. Donl purchase air/ rail/bus tickets through unauthorised travel agents or strangers. Meghalaya Tourism runs regular conducted tours in and around

Shillong. Model Itinerary (Short & Snappy) 1st day — Arrive Guwahati. Drive to Kaziranga. 2nd day — Spend time at Sanctuary/nearby tea-gardens. 3rd day — Drive to Shillong. 4th day — Visit Cherrapunji. 5th day — Tour of Shillong and on to Umiam Lake Resort. Leave for Guwahati. 6th day — Visit to Kamakhya temple early morning. Boat ride on Brahmaputra. Depart for destination. Model Itinerary (Slow & Steady) 1 st day — Arrive Guwahati. Evening free for shopping. 2nd day — After breakfast, drive to Kaziranga, with a lunch break at Nawgong. 3rd & 4th days — Spend time at Sanctuary/nearby tea-gardens. 5th day — Drive to Shillong. 6th day — Shillong sight-seeing. Evening free for shopping. 7th day — Visit Cherrapunji. 8th day — After a spot of Golf, spend rest of the day at Umiam Lake Resort. 9th day — Leave for Guwahati. Visit Umananda on the Brah- maputra. 1 0th day — Visit Kamakhya temple early morning. Depart for des- tination.

The beginning of ever unpredictable Calcutta in 1690, ofcourse ! Today, more than 300 years later, it stHI carries the aura of days gone by — of times when phaetons and victorias drove in state and Englishmen took afternoon drives to the club where they reclined in punkah cooled rooms to discuss trade. Calcutta, then the gateway to India, was the hub of the British India Company. Even after the transfer of the capital to Delhi in 1912, Calcutta is still a many splendoured metropolis. The Indian renaissance started here and India's freedom struggle was born here. Culturally alive, it is home to various modern movements in art, cinema and theatre. Its Noble Laureates include Rabindranath Tagore, Sir C.V. Raman and Mother Teresa. Calcutta is also proud of Satyajit Ray and Ravi Shankar. Calcutta, with over 1 0.5 million people, is a fascinating cosmopolitan brew bubbling with life. There's nothing in Calcutta that you cannot find, and no entertainment surpasses its fare : Antiques, architecture, fine arts, writing, dance, music, drama, the night life, a quiet evening on a boat, religious festivals, soccer or cricket fever and fiery political demonstrations.

Calcutta — the city of joy for ever! If you come here during the festive season (October — November), the city wears a radiant look. The mood is infectious; the spirit, sweeping! Calcutta could well be the key to the understanding of India and is the springboard to West Bengal, the Andamans, Orissa, Bihar and especially the North East. There has been continued two way traffic between Calcutta and Shillong for long. Tagore wrote two of his finest works, ’Gora' ,& 'Shesher Kobita' at Shillong where memorial tablets at Upland Road and Rilbong celebrate the National Bard. Today, international and domestic tourists, Governmental and com- mercial travellers emanate mostly from Calcutta to Shillong while Shiilongites hold Calcutta dear to heart for their Banking, Commercial* Communication, Corporate, Health, Industrial and Media needs. The petition was granted It was also decided that the railway should be extended to the Makum Coalfields across Dihing river. May 1,1881 : Hard toil. Dedication. Sacrifice. All combined to make the inaugural run of the first metre gauge locomotive in Assam possible. 1889 : Oil was struck at Digboi A decade later, the Assam Railway and Trading Company was incorporated. 1910 : At the century's turn, the Assam Bengal Railway was extended to link Assam with the

seaboard at Chittagong. The Eastern Bengal Railway network to Amingaon and Gauhati was completed. Events flowed swiftly with the World Wars, the Partition, Independence and the Five Year Plans— changing the priorities. Today the amalgamated Northeast Frontier Railway, apart from carrying all the coal, tea and oil to and from the country's strategic Northeast, provides the region's most important surface link with the mainland It is the life line, not only for Assam, but for the whole of Northeastern India. § NORTHEAST FRONTIER RAILWAY at your service Rail Travel Information GUWAHATl (103 kms.) is the nearest Railway Station. Surrounded by hills on the other sides, Guwahati — the capital of Assam and the only city in the North East — is the gateway to this enchanting region of unspoilt natural beauty.

Guwahati is well connected by air, rail and road. Regular air and rail services from Calcutta and Delhi are available. Of late East West Airlines has also introduced a flight from Calcutta to Guwahati. Once at Guwahati, a well balanced air, rail and road network helps the most discerning traveller to reach every nook and cranny of the North East. Accommodation at Guwahati — be it star category or budget — is plentiful. The star category hotels include Belle Vue, Brahmaputra Ashok, Chillarai, Dynasty, Nandan, Raj Palace (veg.) and Rituraj. In the middle rung are Ambarish, Kuber (veg.), Mayur (veg.), Nova etc while the budget hotels are Ambassador, Indiraj, Maruti (veg.). Starline, Trimurti etc. The Tourist Bungalow is also excellent at its price. While most of the above hotels offer superior multi-cuisine choice, mention may be made of Ming Room for its Chinese fare, Woodland for its South Indian delicacies, Kalpana Hotel for its Bengali meals and the Paradise Restaurant for its ethnic Assamese lhali’s. Well- known brands of aereated & mineral waters, ice-creams and alcoholic beverages are readily available. Transportation within the town is easy with Governmental and privately owned buses & mini buses. Cycle-rickshaws, auto-rickshaws and taxis are also available, almost round the clock, but it is advisable to bargain and settle the fares in advance. The offices of Assam Tourism (near the Railway Station) and Indian Tourism (at B.K.K. Road, Ulubari) are open everyday from 10AM to 5 PM (barring

Sundays & holidays) to help newcomers. Once at Guwahati, it is customary to visit the Kamakhya Temple, which, set atop the Nilachal Hills, is a vital centre of Hinduism and Shaktism. The view of Guwahati and the Brahmaputra from the Bhubaneshwari Temple area here, is indeed exhilarating. Umananda, 31 Mullah Dervish of Herat who bad accompanied the Mugal General Mir Jumlah to Assam in the middle of the 17th century exclaimed- “Its land is not like our land, Its sky is not like our sky , .... Its sky sends rains down - without the oeriginating cause of the clouds. It stands outside the circle of the earth and the bowels of the enveloping sphere. It has been separated from the world like the letter aliph. The landscape of Assam has changed a lot since then. And Yet the charm and the wonder, the enigma and the mystery associated with her nature lingers on. This land of myth and mystery always backons you

For the general man on the street, Guwahati is the big city with a bigger heart. English, Assamese, Bengali and Hindi are readily spoken and understood here, while a feeling of easy bonhomie helps the outsider feel absolutely at ease. So in order to recover the maximum out of a tyre, retreading is the only option and precured Retreading is the wise and economic choice. TYPES OF RETREADING AVAILABLE There are two types of retreading namely, Conventional Hot Process and Precured Cold Process Currently the conventional Process of mould retreading is in vogue, with the need for more retreads and mileage per tyre. New methods of retreading have been developed in advanced countries and Precured retreading has proved to be the best technology. ADVANTAGES WITH PRECURED RETREADING In Precured retreading process the tyres are retreaded in free road running conditions through out the process* Here the tyres are buffed to a flat surface and the cuts are repaired by scientific methods. The Precured treads are then built on the casing and methods. The Precured treads are then built on the casing and bonded in free size chambers on to the tyres. The tyres do not undergo direct heat as they are covered by thick Butyl envelopes which help in holding the tread to the tyre and distributing the heat uniformly on the crown portion of the tyre during the Bonding process. Advantages of Precured Retreading over Hot Process can be listed broadly as follows :

1. Longer life of casing 2. More Retreads 3. High Mileage 4. Lowest Tread Failure 5. Excellent Balance & Better Traction 6. World renowned Proven Technology 7. Wide choice of tread patterns 8. Advance tyre repair system Due to the above advantages ELGITREAD Precured retreading has been well acepted by the State Transport undertakings, * Fleet operators and also private car owners for all types of ' vehicles, all over the World. Road Travel Information SHILLONG is connected to GUWAHATI by the excellently maintained, all weather National Highway No. 40. It takes nearly 3.5 hours by bus and 3 hours by car to cover the distance - inclusive of a halt at Nongpoh, the half-way house, for tea and snacks or bites of fresh, juicy fruits. The journey is made pleasurable by the picturesque scenery inclusive of Reserve Forests, waterfalls, quaint little villages, gushing mountain streams and of course, the Umiam Lake, 16 kms before reaching Shillong. Khasi-Pnars believe that God made 16 families, Ki Khathynrew Trep (16 huts) and let them stay with him in heaven. Initially, they travelled at will between heaven and earth using a golden ladder. At a certain point of time seven of these families wished to stay back on earth. God agreed and gave them land at Mount Sohpetbneng (literally, the navel of Heaven) but withdrew the golden ladder. Since then the Khasi Hills have become the sacred homeland of the Ki Hynniew Trep, the people of the 7 huts. They have not forgotten the 9 families who stayed back in Heaven and whenever they pray, they request the 9 families to forgive them for their omissions and commissions. Shillong derives its name from the Shillong Peak (6450 feet above sea level) the highest point in Meghalaya, overlooking the Shillong city. There are many legends and myths • surrounding the name of Shillong. According to one legend, the city got its name from a mythical youth, U Shulong, a supernatural youth born out of immaculate conception of a virgin mother named Lir, who lived in Bisi, a village near Mylliem, 14 km south of Shillong. Lir gave birth to a beautiful still-born child, whom she buried in her garden. Many years later she was awakened near midnight by the noise of a large crowd. As she opened her door, a tall, handsome youth stepped forward and said, "Mother, I am the little boy that you buried in the garden. Don't be afraid, you are my earthly mother and I love you. I have come so that all our people can prosper and live happily. Go, call the uncles and the kith and kin so that I may instruct them on how to perform the ceremonies and so that I can be of help

at times of need". U Shulong (the one who grows naturally) was in fact the presiding deity of Shillong and the phrase "Khot Shillong" (Call Shillong) is still used as a prayer and supplication to bring succour in times of catastrophe, peril or or even personal misfortune. The other legend is related with the emergence of the Shillong kingdom in olden times. Even today there is a cave called "Krem MaraT near Shillong peak. This cave was supposed to be the home of the Shillong deity, a supernatural being like a Greek God. People were in great awe of him and tried to propitiate him by sacrificial offerings and ritualistic obeisance, and he bestowed health and wealth upon those whom he preferred. Cowherds and people passing the area would sometime see this unearthly beauty sunning herself, enjoying the shade of a nearby tree or sitting on a ledge. As evening approached the woman would retire into the cave which no human dared to approach. A nobleman of the Mylliemngap clan, who initially dismissed the story as a figment of imagination, decided to find out and hid himself at night at a vantage point near the cave. At daybreak, Mylliemngap, wide awake, after a fitful night, was stunned to see a celestial beauty inhaling and caressing a lovely wild flower, Hew Jalyngkteng, in a very graceful manner. Mylliemngap understood that this was the daughter of the Shillong diety and felt that her appearance was due to divine dispensation to play some specific role in this world. By then the woman had disappeared into the cave. In a bid to lure out the woman from the cave. Mylliemngap tied a bunch of Jalyngkteng flowers at the tip of a long bamboo pole and thrust it inside the cave. The pole quivered and as he pulled it out slowly - lo and behold - the woman was following it out of the cave. As soon as she came out of the cave, Mylliemngap clasped her hand firmly and refused to let her go back into the cave. The woman, know in history as Pahsyntiew (Lured by flower) became the ancestress queen mother of the Shillong kingdom following her marriage to Kongor Nongjri and made the beginning of the royal family

with a progeny of two sons and daughter. Pahsyntiew is credited with teaching her people the science of iron smelting and a new form of agriculture. She. also taught social etiquette and helped her subjects learn to talk, sing and dance. On completion of her human responsibilities, she once more entered the Marai cave never to return, lending credence to the belief that she was in fact the divine daughter of the diety of Shillong. The Shillong Story The story of Shillong actually began at Cherrapunji, the first headquarters of the Khasi and Jaintia Hills district under the Assam Division of the province of Bengal. The serving British officers found the place unhealthy due to heavy rain, mist and fog and above all enteric fever that took heavy toll of the officers, including David Scott, the founder of British suzereignty in these hills. Most of them died there before reaching the age of thirty as the cluster of graveyards still testify. The officers not only had complained to their higher authorities but were also in search of a drier and healthier place for building up a sanatorium where they could retire for recouping their health. Capt. Lister, Political Agent, even surveyed three places, including Mairang in the district, for a likely sanatorium. Meanwhile, as early as the 14th October, 1856, J.AIIen, Member of the Board of Revenue of the Bengal government, apparently responding to the grievances of the officers, recommended shifting of the district headquarters from Cherrapunji to a more suitable place. The area, known today as Upper Shillong, lying at the foot of the Shillong Peak, was selected as the site of the next district

headquarters and sanatorium, but the site had to be abandoned mainly because there was no source of adequate water supply for the people of the projected town. The choice ultimately fell on lewduh, as the area was known then, lewduh also lay on the cart track from Guwahati, then Divisional headquarters, to Cherrapunji. Col. Henry Hopkinson, then Commissioner of Assam Division and Agent to the Governor General, who actually fathered the town of Shillong, took up measures in right earnest for building up the town and shifting the district headquarters from Cherrapunji. He directed Capt. Rowlat, the Deputy Commissioner of the district to proceed to lewduh in 1861. Capt. Rowlat built a cottage for his stay at lewduh and made a detailed survey of the area for the projected town. Col. Hopkinson also sanctioned Rs. 35,000 for the improvement of the Guwahati-lewduh cart road. The final selection of lewduh as the site for the new town was communicated by a letter of December 18, 1863, to the Bengal government, which in its turn approved purchase of land for the purpose. Col. Hopkinson purchased 2499 acres of land at a cost of Rs. 8,433, including Rs. 1,000 paid to 45 CUWAHATl’S EXCLUSIVE FASHION STORE Designer Collections from the Syiem of Mylliem for renouncing all claims to the purchased land. This was the area on which Government buildings began to be constructed. Col. Hopkinson named the town Shillong. The construction took longer than expected and the shifting of

the district headquarters from Cherrapunji, earlier scheduled in 1864, was delayed by two years. It was only on April 28, 1866, that the Deputy Commissioner's office, Treasury, Jail and Police started functioning at Shillong. Counting from that date, Shillong should be 128 years old this year. No other State capital in the country has undergone change of status and fortune as Shillong since its foundation. In February, 1874, on the formation of Assam as a separate province, Shillong was chosen as capital of the new province on account of its salubrious climate and conveniently central situation between the Brahmaputra Valley and the Surma valley. The site of the present Raj Bhavan was then purchased from Mr. Bivar, former D.C. of the district who owned this property, at a cost of Rs. 26,000 for the construction of the official residence of the Chief Commissioner of the province. The road below the present Raj Bhavan along the lake still bears the name of Bivar. Prior to 1897 most of the public offices and private houses of the town were built of rough hewn masonry. The earth quake of June 12, 1897, reduced them in a heap of ruins in the space of few seconds, wrecked the water supply and destroyed the stone masonry embankment that dammed up the water of the artificial Ward's Lake built by the Chief Commissioner Sir William Ward in 1893-94 below the government house. The pent up water of the lake rushing through the breached embankment down the nullah towards the Polo Ground washed away a wooden bridge over it.

The quake occurred at 5 o'clock on Saturday afternoon when almost everyone was out of doors after a rain drenched day. Only two Europeans and 27 Indians were killed in the tremor. When the town was rebuilt, on the advice of a Japanese architect, the buildings were all light structures built on wooden frames and wooden floors. In 1905 following the partition of Bengal and formation of the new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, Dhaka became the capital of the new province. Shillong, however, became the summer capital. After annulment of the partition of Bengal and consequently of the Eastern Bengal and Assam province in 1911, Assam. was revived as a separate province and Shillong again became the capital in 1912. ANTHONY'S COLLEGE Issued by: Director, Public Instruction, Government of Meghalaya The People KHASI-PNARS (a combination signifying the KHASIS and the JAINTIAS) who inhabit the Khasi and the Jaintia Hills are the larger group of indigenous inhabitants of Meghalaya. Belonging to the Austro-Asiatic race of settlers in this region, the Khasi-Pnars are different than other tribes of the north-eastern region who mostly belong to the Tibeto-Burman stock. Theories trace the origion of the Khasi language to the Khmer language of the far east. Many of their customs like shaving of a child's head, chewing of betel and pan, the status of women in the society are similar. They were the first tribe to be exposed to the British rule in the 19th century and the first to have well established business transactions with the neighbouring plains districts on the north and south of their hills. Today, more than a century later, the Khasi-Pnars have features of both the worlds-the simple village culture with a distinctly tribal world-view and the more sophisticated urban culture of which Shillong is the clearest manifestation. You have here both a tribal chairperson of the UPSC as well as a village rustic who has yet to see a TV The Khasi society is not one compact whole. Especially before the advent of Christianity and the development of the written

language, it was fragmented in many ways. It was called a land of " thirty kings and twelve Dolois", the latter one being another form of a ruler in the Jaintia Hills. It was divided politically, dialectically (dialects differ from village to village) and worship of different local deities in different places. Amongst the Khasis we have the Wars on the southernmost part of the district, the Khynriams are settled in the Shillong plateau, the Bhois in the valley towards the north and the Marams in the western ranges of the Khasi hills. The War-Jaintias, a community of the Jaintias (Pnars), living in areas bordering Bangladesh, still have an unwritten dialect. The Pnars occupy the rest of the Jaintia Hills district. One important characteristic of the War-jaintias is their, expertise in the cultivation of pan leaf. This has earned them distinction even in Bangladesh where tens of thousands of them are residing now. Khasi houses, are extremely clean, Khasi housewives are reputed for their hospitality and hard work, sometimes spending major part of the day in housekeeping and keep it spick and span. Most Khasi families are proud of their traditional etiquettes, usually called ' Akor Khasi.' For example, no Khasi boy or girl will walk in front of an elder man without bending, a sign of respect. Children

are taught right from early years about the importance of saying thank you or 'Khublei ' after receiving any gift, and also while giving or receiving something the right hand should always be used. A person is considered extremely uncourteous if he or she hands over money or a piece of paper to any person by gripping it between two fingers. For a Khasi this is a sign of bad behaviour. Paper or money ought to be always handled between the right thumb and other fingers. The most significant Khasi etiquette is the offering of betelnut and pan leaf (Kwai and tympew) to any visitor. This is done by all, rich and poor, irrespective of whether the visitor is a neighbour or outsider, a Khasi or a non-Khasi. So while you visit this part of India, remember that to go back without receiving your due share of Kwai and tympew means your visit is incomplete. THE GAROS, who call themselves A-chik meaning hillmen, are the other major indigenous tribe of the state constituting about 30% of its total population. Anthropologically they differ from the Khasis and the Jaintias as they belong to the Greater Bodo tribe of Tibeto- Burman stock. Perhaps their only similarity with the Khasi society is their matriiineal social system. Comparatively the Garos are more nomadic and thus less isolated. About one lakh Garos live in Bangladesh, quite a large population of them in Coochbehar, about 50,000 in Tripura and nearly one lakh in Assam. The entire Garo society consists of five exogamous divisions- Sangma, Marak, Momin, Areng and Shira, each Garo being member

of one of these Ma'chong or clans. The members of the same clan are 'Maharis' or relatives by matriliny. The Nokpante (Bachelors' dormitory ) is an important part of the Garo society. Here the Garo youths are expected to get their training in music, art and vocations. With the coming of Christianity, this institution is gradually disappearing. Whereas the Khasis offer betelnut and pan to their visitors, in

the Garo homes, rice beer is offered on arrival of an outsider into the house. In marriage, initiative for negotiation comes from the girl's side. Many Garos still believe in the psycho-physical change of a man or woman to some other forms of animals like tiger, snake etc. The Garos value good name and prestige. Any person who tarnishes his or her good name is heavily fined or beaten, Wangala is the biggest festival of the Garos - a thanks giving ceremony to the deity (Mitde) whose blessings ensure a good crop. Meghalaya also has a large number of other tribes and com- munities like the Mizos, Rabhas, Hajongs, Bengalis, Assamese, Nepalis and the like. Its close connection with Bangladesh and Assam as well as the fact that Shillong had been the capital of the region for many years, it has attracted people from other parts of the country. The Shillong municipality, for example, has a non-tribal population of over 50% and you will find a corner of Kathmandu in Mawprem locality, a slice of Aizawl in Madanrting, a mini Calcutta in Jail Road and polo and even a part of Kerala in various educational and health institutions run by the church. salad. Tourist Spots in and around Shillong SHILLONG, 1 500 meters high, is any visitor's dream come true. Unlike most hill resorts it is neither snow bound in winter or over crowded in summer. In the heart of Shillong is the 100 years old, man made WARD LAKE, a picnic spot where it is possible to while away one's time, boating, having paddle-boat rides or just feeding the fish. The lush* green manicured lawns, seasonal flowers and placid waters knit an ambience of its own. The well laid gardens and mini zoo of the LADY HYDARI PARK add to the pleasure of a stroll in it. Situated close to the park is the CRINOLINE WATERFALLS and Shillong's only swimming pool. There are several waterfalls in and around Shillong. On your way to Shillong, afterthe refreshing cuppa at Nongpoh, look out on your right for the MARGARET FALLS, rushing through green virgin woodland. Just after reaching Shillong, a narrow by-way at Mawlai takes one to a view point from where the 135 meters high BISHOP FALLS and the 120 meters BEADON FALLS can be seen together. Before Shillong's rapid expansion to its present size, Beadon Falls used to generate just enough electricity for the use of old Shillong town. SPREAD EAGLE FALLS is near the MES Headquarters and its roar in the calmness of the hills spells a different music. SWEET FALLS is little beyond Happy Valley, (the home of Assam Regiment, the 58 Gorkha Training Centre and the Assam Rifles) and with a picnic basket thrown in - offers you one of the finest day-excursions in Shillong. The taxis, however, do not run on meters. As per the Government's directive of 1991 the authorised rates are Rs. 6.25 for the first kilometre, Rs. 2.00 for subsequent 1/2 kilometre while detention charges are Re. 0.50 for every 5 minutes or part thereof. It is advisable, therefore, to check up and decide on the fare prior to hiring a taxi. Finally, though it is not approved by the Government, 'Sharetaxis do run on fixed point to point basis and charge a flat rate of Rs.5/ per person. This has possibly resulted in the fact that taxi- drivers often take on extra 'passengers' even after being 'hired' by a specific person. Situated at an elevation of 1,496 metres (5000ft) above mean sea level, the capital city has a bracing climate and is a round-the-year destination for tourists and business travellers. SHILLONG is the political and social hub of Meghalaya and is also the headquarters of Meghalaya's most populous East Khasi Hills District. A modern and vibrant mini-city, Shillong has one of the finest golf-courses in the country and the 116-year old Shillong Club. SHILLONG is headquarters of the North Eastern Council, which celebrated its 21st anniversary last year. Various Defence organisa- tions also call this charming city their home base : the Eastern Air Command, the 58 Gorkha Training Centre, the Assam Regimental Centre, HQ 101 Area and the Assam Rifles - the oldest para-military

force in the country. SHILLONG also boasts of the North Eastern Hill University and the famed Pasteur Institute. This is the official residence of the Governor of Meghalaya while a permanent bench of the Guwahati High Court has also been set up here. SHILLONG is also the head-quarters of North Eastern Electric Power Corporation and the Power Grid Corporation, the Geological Survey of India, Indira Gandhi National Open University, Indian Council of Agricultural Research, the Survey of India and the Income Tax Commissioner, the Catholic and Presbyterian Churches and the Ramakrishna Mission in so far as their activities in the North East are concerned. On the anvil is the Indira Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences which, when functional, will be a boon to the entire North East. SHILLONG is criss crossed by NH 40 and 44 and is just 35 Kms. away from Umroi- the only Airport in the State. It is rather unfortunate that inspite of continued effort, the upgradation of this airport to accept Boeings still appears to be a distant dream. SHILLONG'S communication set up has undergone a sea change once the conventional cross-bar type telephone exchange was replaced by a state of the art E-10B electronic exchange recently. STD booths, Telex and Fax facilities along with major Courier Services are easily available. Shillong AIR has a 100KW Medium Wave Transmitter while a Short Wave North Eastern Service is also beamed from here. As for TV, a 1KW centre has been commissioned

recently. A Coal Depot, scheduled to be completed within a 2 year time-span at Jorabat, to be used by registered coal merchants and NGOs and backed by a reliable, all-weather, modern infrastructure including mechanisation, weighbridges, communication set-up and storage facilities is in the offing. The project, on completion will cater to domestic (especially Cement, Paper & Power industries) and export markets and will hopefully benefit prospective customers due the location being near National Highways 37 and 40, easy accessability to Guwahati and a single sales tax window facility. The major festivals observed are : •Shad Suk Mynslem (AprlFMay) Shad Suk Mynsiem (dance of the happy soul) is of relatively recent revival introduced by Ka Seng Khasi, a cultural body of the Khasi-Pnar

community formed in 1 899. The three-day dance festival, which is thanks- giving to God for His blessings in past years and also a prayer for the same in the years to come, was first performed for two days on February 14-15, 1911 at Weiking field at Jaiaw, Shillong. The festival is heralded in Shillong a month earlier with the beating of drums accompanied with playing of Tangmuri, a shehnai-like musical instrument, in front of the Seng Khasi Hall every Sunday evening. On the first day of the three-day festival, a small procession of male dancers proceeds from the Seng Khasi Hall to the dancing arena at Weiking led by drummers, pipers and flag bearers. The procession entering the Weiking ground through the east gateway continues to dance in the arena for about an hour after which they return to the Seng Khasi Hall. On the second and third days, a prayer is offered to God before the dancers proceed to the Weiking ground. Unlike the Nongkrem festival, no religious rites and sacrifices are involved in Shad Suk Mynsiem. The dance is confined to only virgin girls but both bachelors and married men can participate in the dance. There are six different types of dances out of which four types are open to both male and female dancers. Two types of dances are confined to males only. The girl dancers leave the arena clear for male dancers when these two dances are performed. Behdlenkhlam (July) Behdienkhlam, the most important festival of the Jaintias, is celebrated at Jowai and Tuber in the Jaintia Hills District sometime during the rainy season, normally in July or August. The celebration of this

festival was banned by the British authorities for unknown reasons and was revived in 1948 as a cultural heritage of the people. Poles of great length which have been freshly cut from the forest are held across the stream. People jump on the poles and break them all the while dancing in the muddy water of the pool. The festival of a single village lasts about a week. This festival is observed to honour and offer, sacrifices to their greatest god called Saljong (Sun-God). The festival is initiated right in the field by simple but impressive ceremony known as Rugala. The Rugala is then followed by the ceremony of incense known as 'Sasat Soa'. This is performed inside the house of the Nokma or Chief of the village. The Nokma, amidst burning of incense, beating of drums and chanting of the people, utters a few words of incantation and pours rice -beer and sprinkles rice powder over a collection of field produces offered to the gods. This is immediately followed by drinking, dancing and merry making. Dances of Meghalaya The three major tribes of Meghalaya are Khasis, the Jaintias and the Garos - all of them having their distinct dance forms. The SHAD SUK MYNSIEM, literally meaning "Dances of Happy Soul," is the dance festival of the Khasis and is held in April/May at Mawlai field, Shillong, as a thanks-giving to the Almighty. Only virgin girts can participate unlike the males who may well be married. The dance costumes are of silk and muslin while the jewellery is of 24 carat gold and silver. The NONGKREM DANCE is held in Syiemship of Smit during September/October, exhibits almost the same dance form and is a popular tourist attraction. The I.AHOO is the traditional dance of the Jaintia people. Originally called the CHI PI AH Dance, the present name has evolved from the "hooh-ah-hooh" chant of the performers. A female danseuse is flanked by two male dancers - the maiden representing the custodian

of the family & preserver of the race. The man on the right symbolises the uncle or the protector of family and clan. Dancing on the left is the husband or father considered as the progenitor of a particular family or clan. The lone maiden, dancing in rhythm, symbolises the priestess : care-taker of family and clan, religious rites & rituals. The WANGALA is performed by the Garos during their 100 Drums Festival of the same name. Celebrated following the harvest season, young men and women, clad in colourful finery, dance to the rhythm of drums, flutes and song. It is said that the young drummers and the maidens find opportunity, during this festival, to know each other - and choose their future life-partners. Forests and Wildlife Forests have always been an integral part of the people of the state. Be it for timber, firewood or other forest produce like broomstick, bay leaf, cinnamon, etc., forests have been the source of sustenance to the ever-increasing need of man. However, the rich biodiversity of primary forests are disappearing as they give way to only secondary scrub forests due to their continual exploitation by the people. Forests under the control of the State Government account for only 4.43 percent of the total geographical area but these are about the only areas where there is some greenery left. The rest of the forests which are clan, community or privately owned have been recklessly exploited for agriculture and commercial purposes. The forest types include the sal forests, the mixed moist deciduous forests, the evergreen forests, bamboo forests, pine forests and grass- lands. Some of the important timber species include the sal, pine, gamari titachap, teak and makrisal. Many rare plants which have become endemic to only certain pockets include the pygmy lily, pitcher plant, sundew, wild citrus, some rare bamboos, canes and a number of varieties of orchids including the lady's slipper orchid. Therer are two national parks in the State : Balphakram National Park and Nokrak National Park. The wildlife sanctuaries include the

Nongkhyllem Wildlife Sanctuary and the Siju Wildlife Sanctuary. These form the habitat for a number of the rare and threatened birds and animals. Some of the birds which are unique to the area include the great pied hornbill, kalij pheasant, emerald dove, red jungle .fowl, peacock pheasant, racket tailed drongo, Himalayan golden back wookpecker, black naped oriole. The checklist of mammals includes the binturong, clouded leopard, flying squirrel, golden cat, hispid hare, hoolock gibbon, gaur, tiger and elephant. The Forest Department in the State has been making a lot of efforts in afforestation of the already barren areas with the help and cooperation of the local populace. For the control of pollution in urban areas, erratic rainfall and climate changes, planting of trees in every vacant space and protection of existing forests with its wildlife has become an immediate necessity. An enlightened community geared up for action is the only answer if we are to save whatever is left of our forests. T.T.C.MARAK, I.F.S. Divisional Forest Officer Khasl Hills Division, Shillong. To the south are grasslands with rivers, their pebble banks and islands, spreading as they leave the great forests on the Bhutan hills. The rich bird life is distinctive and abundant. Besides transport for sightseeing within the park, elephant rides and boating on the river are also available. Best time to visit : November - April. Nearest town : Barpeta Road (40 Kms.) MANIPUR The Capital is Imphal.

A land of blue green hills, cascading rapids, carpets of flowers and unwinding rivers. Manipur lies in the eastern most corner of India. Rich with tradition this oval shaped valley is surrounded by an aura of mystery. Legends say that the discovery of Manipur is the result of the delight the gods took in dancing. Polo is said to have originated from Manipur. Sogol Kangjej (Manipur Polo) is the chief sport in the state even today. PLACES OF INTEREST IN AND AROUND IMPHAL SRI GOVINDAJEE TEMPLE — This temple adjoining the palace of the former rulers of Manipur is a historic centre for Vaishnavites. It is a simple and beautiful structure with twin gold domes, a paved court and a large, raised congregation hall. The presiding deity in the centre is flanked by shrines of Balaram and Krishna on one side and Jagannath on the other. KHWAIRAMBAND BAZAR — The market is very special because all the stall-holders are women. Not far from here, is a street where beautiful furniture and cane baskets are sold. Other smaller markets are Singjamei, Kongba, Lamlong, Kwakeithel, Heirangoithong, Tera Keithel and Naoremthong. MANIPUR STATE MUSEUM — This interesting museum near the Polo ground houses Manipur's tribal heritage and a collection of portraits of Manipur's former rulers. WAR CEMETERIES — The British and Indian Army Cemeteries com- memorating those who died in the Second World War are serene and well maintained with little stone markers and bronze plaques recording the glorious sacrifice of the heroes. These graves are maintained by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission. SAHEED MINAR — This tall minar at Bir Tikendrajit Park in the heart of the capital, commemorates the indomitable spirit of Manipurl martyrs who sacrificed their lives while fighting against the British' in 1891. MANIPUR ZOOLOGICAL GARDEN — (6 kms.) West of Imphal is the Zoological Garden at Iroishemba on the Imphal Kangchup Road. The graceful brow-antlered deer, one of the rarest species in the world, can be seen here in sylvan surroundings. KHONGHAMPAT ORCHIDARIUM — (7 kms.) More than 110 varieties of orchids, including several rare species are grown here. Peak season is from April to May. LANGTHABAL — (8 kms.) Overlooking the Manipur University,

amidst jack fruit and pine trees are the relics of an old historic palace, well planned temples and ceremonial houses. BISHNUPUR — (27 kms.) The single-celled, conical roofed temple of Lord Bishnu built in 1467. Interesting for its antiquity and Chinese style design. Also well known for its stoneware production. KAINA — . (29 kms.) A beautiful hillock and a sacred place of the. Hindus. PHUBALA — (40 kms.) A charming resort on a little island, on the western fringes of the Loktak Lake, to the south of Imphal. It is joined with the mainland by a low causeway. MOIRANG — (45 kms.) Here is the ancient temple of the pre-Hindu deity, Lord Thangjlng. It was in Moirang that the flag of the Indian National Army was first hoisted on Indian soil by Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose. The INA Museum here contains letters, photographs, badges of ranks and other articles associated with the movement. LOKTAK LAKE AND SENDRA ISLAND — (48 kms.) A huge and beautiful stretch of water. From the Tourist Bungalow set atop Sendra Island one can get a bird's eye view of the lake and life around it. Gaze at the fishermen as they cast their net, rear fish farms using nets as floating wails or as they build houses on islands of floating weeds. CHIBAI (WELCOME) Nestled deep in the hills, the evergreen forests and pleasant climate of Mizoram beckons tourists from all over the world. Gone are the days of seclusion, and

the lush, verdant hills and green valleys now open their arms wide to give all travellers a warm welcome. The capital, Aizawl, is perched along the hill slopes and offers the visitor a breathtaking view of the land that is Mizoram. The people are peaceful and fun-loving, their colourful clothes brighten the hills which resound to the sound of music and songs that is so much a part of life here. Aizawl is connected by air to Calcutta by Vayudoot. The nearest Rail-head is Silchar, 180 Kms away and connected to Aizawl by NH-54. Both routes will give the tourist a rare and thrilling glimpse of a beautiful vista. The Tourist Lodge at Aizawl is ready and waiting for you with a smile, good service and a ‘CHIBAI’, which means ‘WELCOME’ in Mizo. Visit Mizoram. It's a visit you will never forget. TOURISM DEPARTMENT MIZORAM ISSUED BY ■ DIRECTOR, INFORMATION & PUBLIC RELATIONS, GOVERNMENT OF MIZORAM, AIZAWL ENCHANTING MIZORAM The small state of Mizoram is a place where the hills come alive with the sound of music. It has a distinctive culture of its own, its people firmly rooted to soil, and their

songs, dances and their very lifestyle are all reflections of their self contained unitary lives. Mizoram is a new name given to the mountainous region earlier known as the Lushai Hills. It was one of the districts of Assam till 1972 when it became a Union Territory and later became a full-fledged State on 20th February, 1987. Sandwiched between Burma in the East and South and Bangladesh in the West, Mizoram occupies an area of great strategic importance in the North-Eastern corner of India. The hills in Mizoram runs from North to South with a tendency to be higher in the East of the Territory and tapering in the North and South. The hills are steep and are separated by rivers which flow either to the North or South creating deep gorges between the hill ranges Mizoram has a pleasant climate. It is generally cool in summer and not very cold in winter. The winter skies are wonderfully blue and in the morning the mist forming between the hills gives an

enchanting view of wide stretches resembling a vast lake. This exquisitely picturesque, vibrantly colourful, lush fertile narrow strip of mountain territory covers an area of 1 6,579 sq.kms. The state consists of seven districts with sixteen tribes and sub-tribes who speak English besides Ao, Konyak, Angami, Serna, Lotha and other tribes who have their own dialects. They are said to belong to the Indo-Mongoloid stock, a race whose presence was first noted 10 centuries before Christ. Sanskrit literature describes them as kiratas or hillmen living on nature's gifts, warlike and possessing formidable weapons. The ceremonial dress of each tribe is quite fascinating; the multi- colour spear, ceremonial dao, bracelets, chest plates and head dress of coloured bamboo. Each tribe is proud of the distinguishing colours and patterns woven in their shawls. The tribes are full of folklore and fond of seasonal songs, solo, duet and choric. The most popular ones eulogise ancestors, warriors and traditional heroes. Kohima, the state capital is a hill station, situated at an altitude of 1,495 metres above sea level. It is an enchanting hill town presenting

Tripura, a picturesque hilly region is the second smallest state of India. Covering an area of about 10,500 sq. kms., it was a former princely state. Tripura is bounded on the north, west, south and south-east by international boundary of Bangladesh. In the east, it has a common boundary with Mizoram and Assam. The scenic beauty of Tripura, its forests and lakes and above all its flora and fauna are a delight to the sight. Its rich and varied culture, its handloom and handicraft which is exquisite in colour, excellent in design and craftsmanship, are temptation to the visitor. Tripura is inhabited by various ethnic groups with the cultural heritage of one community differing from another. Inspite of the diverse ethnic groups maintaining their distinct cultural identities, they have mingled into a single whole giving birth to a unique cultural genre. Agartala, the capital is surrounded by hills on three sides. The present site of Agartala was chosen by Maharaja Krishna Kishore Manikya Bahadur who shifted the Capital from old Agartala. To secure labour welfare the Labour Commis- sioner is implementing the rates of minumum wages fixed/revised from time to time for various employ- ments which at present stand at Rs. 25/- per day for unskilled labour and Rs. 30/- per day for skilled labour. There are two Labour Welfare Centres at Sohra

in East Khasi Hills and Mendipathar in East Qaro Hills.. These centres provide elementary training in Sewing, Knitting, and Embroidery and also recrea- tional facilities to workers and their family members. The number of trainees being trained each year is about 50 in both the centres. Issued by the Labour Commissioner, Meghalaya, Shillong. — - — o The Directorate of Employment and Craftsmen Training functions through a net work of Employment Exchanges and Industrial Training Institutes in the State. The Employment Exchanges render employment assis- tance to Job-seekers and provide them with Vocational Guidance and Occupational Information for showing their careers. The Coaching-cum Guidance Centre , Shillong assists the Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes candidates to compete In recruitment conducted by various agencies. The Industrial Training Institutes impart Vocational Training to youths in different trades like Electrician , Motor Mechanic etc. etc. ThelndustrialTraln- ing Institute for Women , Shillong imparts training in the trade of Dress-making. For Foreign Travellers FORMALITIES : As prevalent in the North Eastern Sector, foreign tourists intending to visit Meghalaya require Restricted Area Permits. The applications stating complete details of name, passport number (its issuing authority and the expiry date), place of birth, profession, duration of stay and the

purpose of visit, should be addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, North Block, New Delhi 110001, well in advance of undertaking the trip. However, the Foreigners' Regional Registration Officers of the Government of India at New Delhi, Bombay, Calcutta and Madras are authorised to grant Restricted Area Permits to organised groups of foreign tourists. This, however, is subject to the condition that the visits are confined strictly to Shillong, Cherrapunjee, Barapani, Mawsynram, Jakrem, Ranikor, Thadlaskein, Nartiang, Tura & Slju. Permitted foreign tourists have to travel to Guwahati and back by air and then travel by a prescribed route to these places. They have to visit in groups, minimum of four members, their duration of stay cannot exceed ten days and visits are to be organised only by recognised travel agencies. DO'S AND DON'TS Photography at airports is prohibited. Foreign nationals can pay their hotel bills in foreign cuuency, in Indian Rupees or by travellers cheques. Exchange your money only through authorised banks/money changers, or you may find yourself with counterfeit money. Insist on a receipt when exchanging your money. Retain all exchange receipts with you as without them, you cannot reconvert your unspent money on your final departure from India. Export of most wildlife and their products is banned or strictly regulated. Insist on getting a certificate for the legitimate purchase of

articles made of a particular animal product and permission for its export. Export of antiques over 100 years old is prohibited. While shopping, avoid touts and brokers. It UVE VIBRANT EXCITING New Frontier Colour Lab (P) Ltd. Regd. Office and Lab : S.S. Road. Lakhtokia, (iuwahati 1 Phone : 34686, 544011 Travel Tips Shillong is cosmopolitan in nature. Local customs and etiquette have been dealt with seperately in this book. Living conditions range from star-category hotels to budget ones. Tourist Bungalow and Youth Hostel facilities are also available. It is advisable to make travel arrangements in advance especially if you are planning to travel within September to May (the high tourist season). Do include one or two more destinations in your itinerary, say Guwahati and Kaziranga, so as to get a real taste of the North East. Try to fit in a fair or festival and let your senses exhilarate to the colours and gaiety. English is understood and spoken in Meghalaya. Assamese, Bengali, Hindi and Nepali are also spoken. We have devoted some space to the usage of Khasi which is the local language. Meghalayans are hospitable and friendly people, never need a tourist be lost on the streets. Someone will always help you reach

your destination. Professional help is readily available from the Govt, of India and Meghalaya Tourism staff. It is always advisable to carry packed lunch and bottled drinks when setting out for the day. ('Avomine 1 tablets are definite help for those suffering from travel sickness.) If you have a weak stomach, stick to mineral water, bottled drinks, coffee, tea, beer or wine during meals. Tap water is not always chlorinated. In case you fall sick, Shillong has excellent doctors, chemists and hospitals. Ask your hotel to recommend a doctor if you ever need one. Always remember to pack an umbrella - rains are a normal day-do-day matter. Bring your camera and colour films by all means. Meghalaya has a lot to offer to the nature lover. Colour films and processing facilities are easily available at Shillong. It is safe to travel within Meghalaya. Even if you read of some trouble at times, do not be discouraged, as these are stray incidents. Credit Cards are accepted by hotels, travel agents, shops and restaurants. 10% tipping is customary in case your hotel bills do not include service charges. This would come down to 5% if you are travelling with a group. Taxis in Shillong do not run on meters. Take help of your hotel receptionist and settle the taxi fare in advance. Donl purchase air/ rail/bus tickets through unauthorised travel agents or strangers. Meghalaya Tourism runs regular conducted tours in and around

Shillong. Model Itinerary (Short & Snappy) 1st day — Arrive Guwahati. Drive to Kaziranga. 2nd day — Spend time at Sanctuary/nearby tea-gardens. 3rd day — Drive to Shillong. 4th day — Visit Cherrapunji. 5th day — Tour of Shillong and on to Umiam Lake Resort. Leave for Guwahati. 6th day — Visit to Kamakhya temple early morning. Boat ride on Brahmaputra. Depart for destination. Model Itinerary (Slow & Steady) 1 st day — Arrive Guwahati. Evening free for shopping. 2nd day — After breakfast, drive to Kaziranga, with a lunch break at Nawgong. 3rd & 4th days — Spend time at Sanctuary/nearby tea-gardens. 5th day — Drive to Shillong. 6th day — Shillong sight-seeing. Evening free for shopping. 7th day — Visit Cherrapunji. 8th day — After a spot of Golf, spend rest of the day at Umiam Lake Resort. 9th day — Leave for Guwahati. Visit Umananda on the Brah- maputra. 1 0th day — Visit Kamakhya temple early morning. Depart for des- tination.

Today, more than 300 years later, it stHI carries the aura of days gone by — of times when phaetons and victorias drove in state and Englishmen took afternoon drives to the club where they reclined in punkah cooled rooms to discuss trade. Calcutta, then the gateway to India, was the hub of the British India Company. Even after the transfer of the capital to Delhi in 1912, Calcutta is still a many splendoured metropolis. The Indian renaissance started here and India's freedom struggle was born here. Culturally alive, it is home to various modern movements in art, cinema and theatre. Its Noble Laureates include Rabindranath Tagore, Sir C.V. Raman and Mother Teresa. Calcutta is also proud of Satyajit Ray and Ravi Shankar. Calcutta, with over 1 0.5 million people, is a fascinating cosmopolitan brew bubbling with life. There's nothing in Calcutta that you cannot find, and no entertainment surpasses its fare : Antiques, architecture, fine arts, writing, dance, music, drama, the night life, a quiet evening on a boat, religious festivals, soccer or cricket fever and fiery political demonstrations.

Calcutta — the city of joy for ever! If you come here during the festive season (October — November), the city wears a radiant look. The mood is infectious; the spirit, sweeping! Calcutta could well be the key to the understanding of India and is the springboard to West Bengal, the Andamans, Orissa, Bihar and especially the North East. There has been continued two way traffic between Calcutta and Shillong for long. Tagore wrote two of his finest works, ’Gora' ,& 'Shesher Kobita' at Shillong where memorial tablets at Upland Road and Rilbong celebrate the National Bard. Surrounded by hills on the other sides, Guwahati — the capital of Assam and the only city in the North East — is the gateway to this enchanting region of unspoilt natural beauty.

Guwahati is well connected by air, rail and road. Regular air and rail services from Calcutta and Delhi are available. Of late East West Airlines has also introduced a flight from Calcutta to Guwahati. Once at Guwahati, a well balanced air, rail and road network helps the most discerning traveller to reach every nook and cranny of the North East. Accommodation at Guwahati — be it star category or budget — is plentiful. The star category hotels include Belle Vue, Brahmaputra Ashok, Chillarai, Dynasty, Nandan, Raj Palace (veg.) and Rituraj. In the middle rung are Ambarish, Kuber (veg.), Mayur (veg.), Nova etc while the budget hotels are Ambassador, Indiraj, Maruti (veg.). Starline, Trimurti etc. The Tourist Bungalow is also excellent at its price. While most of the above hotels offer superior multi-cuisine choice, mention may be made of Ming Room for its Chinese fare, Woodland for its South Indian delicacies, Kalpana Hotel for its Bengali meals and the Paradise Restaurant for its ethnic Assamese lhali’s. Well- known brands of aereated & mineral waters, ice-creams and alcoholic beverages are readily available. Transportation within the town is easy with Governmental and privately owned buses & mini buses. Cycle-rickshaws, auto-rickshaws and taxis are also available, almost round the clock, but it is advisable to bargain and settle the fares in advance. The offices of Assam Tourism (near the Railway Station) and Indian Tourism (at B.K.K. Road, Ulubari) are open everyday from 10AM to 5 PM (barring

Sundays & holidays) to help newcomers. Once at Guwahati, it is customary to visit the Kamakhya Temple, which, set atop the Nilachal Hills, is a vital centre of Hinduism and Shaktism. The view of Guwahati and the Brahmaputra from the Bhubaneshwari Temple area here, is indeed exhilarating. Umananda, 31 Mullah Dervish of Herat who bad accompanied the Mugal General Mir Jumlah to Assam in the middle of the 17th century exclaimed- “Its land is not like our land, Its sky is not like our sky , .... Its sky sends rains down - without the oeriginating cause of the clouds. It stands outside the circle of the earth and the bowels of the enveloping sphere. It has been separated from the world like the letter aliph. The landscape of Assam has changed a lot since then. And Yet the charm and the wonder, the enigma and the mystery associated with her nature lingers on. This land of myth and mystery always backons you

with modern studios and recording centres. It is also home to Dr. Bhupen Hazarika, recently honoured by the Phalke award. AIR and Doordarshan have their regional head quarters here as do so many other Central Government organisations. As the capital of North East's most politically and economically mature State, both national and regional political parties have their presence here. For the general man on the street, Guwahati is the big city with a bigger heart. English, Assamese, Bengali and Hindi are readily spoken and understood here, while a feeling of easy bonhomie helps the outsider feel absolutely at ease. So in order to recover the maximum out of a tyre, retreading is the only option and precured Retreading is the wise and economic choice. TYPES OF RETREADING AVAILABLE There are two types of retreading namely, Conventional Hot Process and Precured Cold Process Currently the conventional Process of mould retreading is in vogue, with the need for more retreads and mileage per tyre. New methods of retreading have been developed in advanced countries and Precured retreading has proved to be the best technology. ADVANTAGES WITH PRECURED RETREADING In Precured retreading process the tyres are retreaded in free road running conditions through out the process* Here the tyres are buffed to a flat surface and the cuts are repaired by scientific methods. The Precured treads are then built on the casing and methods. The Precured treads are then built on the casing and bonded in free size chambers on to the tyres. The tyres do not undergo direct heat as they are covered by thick Butyl envelopes which help in holding the tread to the tyre and distributing the heat uniformly on the crown portion of the tyre during the Bonding process. Advantages of Precured Retreading over Hot Process can be listed broadly as follows :

1. Longer life of casing 2. More Retreads 3. High Mileage 4. Lowest Tread Failure 5. Excellent Balance & Better Traction 6. World renowned Proven Technology 7. Wide choice of tread patterns 8. Advance tyre repair system Due to the above advantages ELGITREAD Precured retreading has been well acepted by the State Transport undertakings, * Fleet operators and also private car owners for all types of ' vehicles, all over the World. Road Travel Information SHILLONG is connected to GUWAHATI by the excellently maintained, all weather National Highway No. 40. It takes nearly 3.5 hours by bus and 3 hours by car to cover the distance - inclusive of a halt at Nongpoh, the half-way house, for tea and snacks or bites of fresh, juicy fruits. The journey is made pleasurable by the picturesque scenery inclusive of Reserve Forests, waterfalls, quaint little villages, gushing mountain streams and of course, the Umiam Lake, 16 kms before reaching Shillong. Various forms of surface transport are available. Khasi-Pnars believe that God made 16 families, Ki Khathynrew Trep (16 huts) and let them stay with him in heaven. Initially, they travelled at will between heaven and earth using a golden ladder. At a certain point of time seven of these families wished to stay back on earth. God agreed and gave them land at Mount Sohpetbneng (literally, the navel of Heaven) but withdrew the golden ladder. Since then the Khasi Hills have become the sacred homeland of the Ki Hynniew Trep, the people of the 7 huts. They have not forgotten the 9 families who stayed back in Heaven and whenever they pray, they request the 9 families to forgive them for their omissions and commissions. Shillong derives its name from the Shillong Peak (6450 feet above sea level) the highest point in Meghalaya, overlooking the Shillong city. There are many legends and myths • surrounding the name of Shillong. According to one legend, the city got its name from a mythical youth, U Shulong, a supernatural youth born out of immaculate conception of a virgin mother named Lir, who lived in Bisi, a village near Mylliem, 14 km south of Shillong. Lir gave birth to a beautiful still-born child, whom she buried in her garden. Many years later she was awakened near midnight by the noise of a large crowd. As she opened her door, a tall, handsome youth stepped forward and said, "Mother, I am the little boy that you buried in the garden. Don't be afraid, you are my earthly mother and I love you. I have come so that all our people can prosper and live happily. Go, call the uncles and the kith and kin so that I may instruct them on how to perform the ceremonies and so that I can be of help

at times of need". U Shulong (the one who grows naturally) was in fact the presiding deity of Shillong and the phrase "Khot Shillong" (Call Shillong) is still used as a prayer and supplication to bring succour in times of catastrophe, peril or or even personal misfortune. The other legend is related with the emergence of the Shillong kingdom in olden times. Even today there is a cave called "Krem MaraT near Shillong peak. This cave was supposed to be the home of the Shillong deity, a supernatural being like a Greek God. People were in great awe of him and tried to propitiate him by sacrificial offerings and ritualistic obeisance, and he bestowed health and wealth upon those whom he preferred. Cowherds and people passing the area would sometime see this unearthly beauty sunning herself, enjoying the shade of a nearby tree or sitting on a ledge. As evening approached the woman would retire into the cave which no human dared to approach. A nobleman of the Mylliemngap clan, who initially dismissed the story as a figment of imagination, decided to find out and hid himself at night at a vantage point near the cave. At daybreak, Mylliemngap, wide awake, after a fitful night, was stunned to see a celestial beauty inhaling and caressing a lovely wild flower, Hew Jalyngkteng, in a very graceful manner. Mylliemngap understood that this was the daughter of the Shillong diety and felt that her appearance was due to divine dispensation to play some specific role in this world. By then the woman had disappeared into the cave. In a bid to lure out the woman from the cave. Mylliemngap tied a bunch of Jalyngkteng flowers at the tip of a long bamboo pole and thrust it inside the cave. The pole quivered and as he pulled it out slowly - lo and behold - the woman was following it out of the cave. As soon as she came out of the cave, Mylliemngap clasped her hand firmly and refused to let her go back into the cave. The woman, know in history as Pahsyntiew (Lured by flower) became the ancestress queen mother of the Shillong kingdom following her marriage to Kongor Nongjri and made the beginning of the royal family

with a progeny of two sons and daughter. Pahsyntiew is credited with teaching her people the science of iron smelting and a new form of agriculture. She. also taught social etiquette and helped her subjects learn to talk, sing and dance. On completion of her human responsibilities, she once more entered the Marai cave never to return, lending credence to the belief that she was in fact the divine daughter of the diety of Shillong. The Shillong Story The story of Shillong actually began at Cherrapunji, the first headquarters of the Khasi and Jaintia Hills district under the Assam Division of the province of Bengal. The serving British officers found the place unhealthy due to heavy rain, mist and fog and above all enteric fever that took heavy toll of the officers, including David Scott, the founder of British suzereignty in these hills. Most of them died there before reaching the age of thirty as the cluster of graveyards still testify. The officers not only had complained to their higher authorities but were also in search of a drier and healthier place for building up a sanatorium where they could retire for recouping their health. Capt. Lister, Political Agent, even surveyed three places, including Mairang in the district, for a likely sanatorium. Meanwhile, as early as the 14th October, 1856, J.AIIen, Member of the Board of Revenue of the Bengal government, apparently responding to the grievances of the officers, recommended shifting of the district headquarters from Cherrapunji to a more suitable place. The area, known today as Upper Shillong, lying at the foot of the Shillong Peak, was selected as the site of the next district

headquarters and sanatorium, but the site had to be abandoned mainly because there was no source of adequate water supply for the people of the projected town. The choice ultimately fell on lewduh, as the area was known then, lewduh also lay on the cart track from Guwahati, then Divisional headquarters, to Cherrapunji. Col. Henry Hopkinson, then Commissioner of Assam Division and Agent to the Governor General, who actually fathered the town of Shillong, took up measures in right earnest for building up the town and shifting the district headquarters from Cherrapunji. He directed Capt. Rowlat, the Deputy Commissioner of the district to proceed to lewduh in 1861. Capt. Rowlat built a cottage for his stay at lewduh and made a detailed survey of the area for the projected town. Col. Hopkinson also sanctioned Rs. 35,000 for the improvement of the Guwahati-lewduh cart road. The final selection of lewduh as the site for the new town was communicated by a letter of December 18, 1863, to the Bengal government, which in its turn approved purchase of land for the purpose. Col. Hopkinson purchased 2499 acres of land at a cost of Rs. 8,433, including Rs. 1,000 paid to 45 CUWAHATl’S EXCLUSIVE FASHION STORE Designer Collections from the Syiem of Mylliem for renouncing all claims to the purchased land. This was the area on which Government buildings began to be constructed. Col. Hopkinson named the town Shillong. The construction took longer than expected and the shifting of

the district headquarters from Cherrapunji, earlier scheduled in 1864, was delayed by two years. It was only on April 28, 1866, that the Deputy Commissioner's office, Treasury, Jail and Police started functioning at Shillong. Counting from that date, Shillong should be 128 years old this year. No other State capital in the country has undergone change of status and fortune as Shillong since its foundation. In February, 1874, on the formation of Assam as a separate province, Shillong was chosen as capital of the new province on account of its salubrious climate and conveniently central situation between the Brahmaputra Valley and the Surma valley. The site of the present Raj Bhavan was then purchased from Mr. Bivar, former D.C. of the district who owned this property, at a cost of Rs. 26,000 for the construction of the official residence of the Chief Commissioner of the province. The road below the present Raj Bhavan along the lake still bears the name of Bivar. Prior to 1897 most of the public offices and private houses of the town were built of rough hewn masonry. The earth quake of June 12, 1897, reduced them in a heap of ruins in the space of few seconds, wrecked the water supply and destroyed the stone masonry embankment that dammed up the water of the artificial Ward's Lake built by the Chief Commissioner Sir William Ward in 1893-94 below the government house. The pent up water of the lake rushing through the breached embankment down the nullah towards the Polo Ground washed away a wooden bridge over it.

The quake occurred at 5 o'clock on Saturday afternoon when almost everyone was out of doors after a rain drenched day. Only two Europeans and 27 Indians were killed in the tremor. When the town was rebuilt, on the advice of a Japanese architect, the buildings were all light structures built on wooden frames and wooden floors. In 1905 following the partition of Bengal and formation of the new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, Dhaka became the capital of the new province. Shillong, however, became the summer capital. After annulment of the partition of Bengal and consequently of the Eastern Bengal and Assam province in 1911, Assam. was revived as a separate province and Shillong again became the capital in 1912. ANTHONY'S COLLEGE Issued by: Director, Public Instruction, Government of Meghalaya The People KHASI-PNARS (a combination signifying the KHASIS and the JAINTIAS) who inhabit the Khasi and the Jaintia Hills are the larger group of indigenous inhabitants of Meghalaya. Belonging to the Austro-Asiatic race of settlers in this region, the Khasi-Pnars are different than other tribes of the north-eastern region who mostly belong to the Tibeto-Burman stock. Theories trace the origion of the Khasi language to the Khmer language of the far east. Many of their customs like shaving of a child's head, chewing of betel and pan, the status of women in the society are similar. They were the first tribe to be exposed to the British rule in the 19th century and the first to have well established business transactions with the neighbouring plains districts on the north and south of their hills. Today, more than a century later, the Khasi-Pnars have features of both the worlds-the simple village culture with a distinctly tribal world-view and the more sophisticated urban culture of which Shillong is the clearest manifestation. You have here both a tribal chairperson of the UPSC as well as a village rustic who has yet to see a TV The Khasi society is not one compact whole. Especially before the advent of Christianity and the development of the written

language, it was fragmented in many ways. It was called a land of " thirty kings and twelve Dolois", the latter one being another form of a ruler in the Jaintia Hills. It was divided politically, dialectically (dialects differ from village to village) and worship of different local deities in different places. Amongst the Khasis we have the Wars on the southernmost part of the district, the Khynriams are settled in the Shillong plateau, the Bhois in the valley towards the north and the Marams in the western ranges of the Khasi hills. The War-Jaintias, a community of the Jaintias (Pnars), living in areas bordering Bangladesh, still have an unwritten dialect. The Pnars occupy the rest of the Jaintia Hills district. One important characteristic of the War-jaintias is their, expertise in the cultivation of pan leaf. This has earned them distinction even in Bangladesh where tens of thousands of them are residing now. Khasi houses, are extremely clean, Khasi housewives are reputed for their hospitality and hard work, sometimes spending major part of the day in housekeeping and keep it spick and span. Most Khasi families are proud of their traditional etiquettes, usually called ' Akor Khasi.' For example, no Khasi boy or girl will walk in front of an elder man without bending, a sign of respect. Children

are taught right from early years about the importance of saying thank you or 'Khublei ' after receiving any gift, and also while giving or receiving something the right hand should always be used. A person is considered extremely uncourteous if he or she hands over money or a piece of paper to any person by gripping it between two fingers. For a Khasi this is a sign of bad behaviour. Paper or money ought to be always handled between the right thumb and other fingers. The most significant Khasi etiquette is the offering of betelnut and pan leaf (Kwai and tympew) to any visitor. This is done by all, rich and poor, irrespective of whether the visitor is a neighbour or outsider, a Khasi or a non-Khasi. So while you visit this part of India, remember that to go back without receiving your due share of Kwai and tympew means your visit is incomplete. THE GAROS, who call themselves A-chik meaning hillmen, are the other major indigenous tribe of the state constituting about 30% of its total population. Anthropologically they differ from the Khasis and the Jaintias as they belong to the Greater Bodo tribe of Tibeto- Burman stock. Perhaps their only similarity with the Khasi society is their matriiineal social system. Comparatively the Garos are more nomadic and thus less isolated. About one lakh Garos live in Bangladesh, quite a large population of them in Coochbehar, about 50,000 in Tripura and nearly one lakh in Assam. The entire Garo society consists of five exogamous divisions- Sangma, Marak, Momin, Areng and Shira, each Garo being member

of one of these Ma'chong or clans. The members of the same clan are 'Maharis' or relatives by matriliny. salad. Tourist Spots in and around Shillong SHILLONG, 1 500 meters high, is any visitor's dream come true. Unlike most hill resorts it is neither snow bound in winter or over crowded in summer. In the heart of Shillong is the 100 years old, man made WARD LAKE, a picnic spot where it is possible to while away one's time, boating, having paddle-boat rides or just feeding the fish. The lush* green manicured lawns, seasonal flowers and placid waters knit an ambience of its own. The well laid gardens and mini zoo of the LADY HYDARI PARK add to the pleasure of a stroll in it. Situated close to the park is the CRINOLINE WATERFALLS and Shillong's only swimming pool. There are several waterfalls in and around Shillong. On your way to Shillong, afterthe refreshing cuppa at Nongpoh, look out on your right for the MARGARET FALLS, rushing through green virgin woodland. Just after reaching Shillong, a narrow by-way at Mawlai takes one to a view point from where the 135 meters high BISHOP FALLS and the 120 meters BEADON FALLS can be seen together. Before Shillong's rapid expansion to its present size, Beadon Falls used to generate just enough electricity for the use of old Shillong town. SPREAD EAGLE FALLS is near the MES Headquarters and its roar in the calmness of the hills spells a different music. SWEET FALLS is little beyond Happy Valley, (the home of Assam Regiment, the 58 Gorkha Training Centre and the Assam Rifles) and with a picnic basket thrown in - offers you one of the finest day-excursions in Shillong. ELEPHANT

FALLS is a unique two tiered waterfall 1 0 km on the way to Cherrapunji and is a must on the tourist itinerary. SHILLONG PEAK is the highest point in Meghalaya. Situated at an elevation of 1,496 metres (5000ft) above mean sea level, the capital city has a bracing climate and is a round-the-year destination for tourists and business travellers. SHILLONG is the political and social hub of Meghalaya and is also the headquarters of Meghalaya's most populous East Khasi Hills District. A modern and vibrant mini-city, Shillong has one of the finest golf-courses in the country and the 116-year old Shillong Club. SHILLONG is headquarters of the North Eastern Council, which celebrated its 21st anniversary last year. Various Defence organisa- tions also call this charming city their home base : the Eastern Air Command, the 58 Gorkha Training Centre, the Assam Regimental Centre, HQ 101 Area and the Assam Rifles - the oldest para-military

force in the country. SHILLONG also boasts of the North Eastern Hill University and the famed Pasteur Institute. This is the official residence of the Governor of Meghalaya while a permanent bench of the Guwahati High Court has also been set up here. SHILLONG is also the head-quarters of North Eastern Electric Power Corporation and the Power Grid Corporation, the Geological Survey of India, Indira Gandhi National Open University, Indian Council of Agricultural Research, the Survey of India and the Income Tax Commissioner, the Catholic and Presbyterian Churches and the Ramakrishna Mission in so far as their activities in the North East are concerned. On the anvil is the Indira Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences which, when functional, will be a boon to the entire North East. SHILLONG is criss crossed by NH 40 and 44 and is just 35 Kms. away from Umroi- the only Airport in the State. It is rather unfortunate that inspite of continued effort, the upgradation of this airport to accept Boeings still appears to be a distant dream.
