The major festivals observed are : •Shad Suk Mynslem (AprlFMay) Shad Suk Mynsiem (dance of the happy soul) is of relatively recent revival introduced by Ka Seng Khasi, a cultural body of the Khasi-Pnar

community formed in 1 899. The three-day dance festival, which is thanks- giving to God for His blessings in past years and also a prayer for the same in the years to come, was first performed for two days on February 14-15, 1911 at Weiking field at Jaiaw, Shillong. The festival is heralded in Shillong a month earlier with the beating of drums accompanied with playing of Tangmuri, a shehnai-like musical instrument, in front of the Seng Khasi Hall every Sunday evening. On the first day of the three-day festival, a small procession of male dancers proceeds from the Seng Khasi Hall to the dancing arena at Weiking led by drummers, pipers and flag bearers. The procession entering the Weiking ground through the east gateway continues to dance in the arena for about an hour after which they return to the Seng Khasi Hall. On the second and third days, a prayer is offered to God before the dancers proceed to the Weiking ground. Unlike the Nongkrem festival, no religious rites and sacrifices are involved in Shad Suk Mynsiem. The dance is confined to only virgin girls but both bachelors and married men can participate in the dance. There are six different types of dances out of which four types are open to both male and female dancers. Two types of dances are confined to males only. The girl dancers leave the arena clear for male dancers when these two dances are performed. Behdlenkhlam (July) Behdienkhlam, the most important festival of the Jaintias, is celebrated at Jowai and Tuber in the Jaintia Hills District sometime during the rainy season, normally in July or August. The celebration of this

festival was banned by the British authorities for unknown reasons and was revived in 1948 as a cultural heritage of the people. The three-day festival begins with religious rites which indude sacrifices to ’U Mukhai', food offerings to departed souls of ancestors, chasing away the evils and dancing in which the young and the old take part. On the last day in the morning the townsflok led by the 'Oolof move about beating the roof of every house with sticks driving away the plague from the house. Later in th& afternoon, well decorated 'rots', look-alikes of tazias brought out during Muslim festival of Mohurram, one each from the seven localities of the town are brought on the bank of a pool formed by a stream where 'Aitnar' dwells. Poles of great length which have been freshly cut from the forest are held across the stream. People jump on the poles and break them all the while dancing in the muddy water of the pool. Later a large pole is placed across the stream, and the people dividing themselves into two parties gopd humouredly contend for the possession of this pole. The concluding part of the festival is 'Katlawakor' much like a game of football, which is played between two parties, one representing the upper valley and the other the lower valley of the Myntdu river, with a wooden ball. Whichever party wins believes they would have better harvest than the other.. WANGALA (October-November) This is the biggest of all the festivals of the Garos performed in connection with the Jhum cultivation. This is usually held in October and

so sometimes it synchronises with the Durga Puja, but each village sets its own time and so there are two or three weeks during which Wangla is celebrated in one or two villages. The festival of a single village lasts about a week. This festival is observed to honour and offer, sacrifices to their greatest god called Saljong (Sun-God). The festival is initiated right in the field by simple but impressive ceremony known as Rugala. The Rugala is then followed by the ceremony of incense known as 'Sasat Soa'. This is performed inside the house of the Nokma or Chief of the village. The Nokma, amidst burning of incense, beating of drums and chanting of the people, utters a few words of incantation and pours rice -beer and sprinkles rice powder over a collection of field produces offered to the gods. This is immediately followed by drinking, dancing and merry making. People young and old, boys and girls, in their colourful costumes with feathered headgear dance to the tunes of music played on long oval shaped drums. Dances of Meghalaya The three major tribes of Meghalaya are Khasis, the Jaintias and the Garos - all of them having their distinct dance forms. The SHAD SUK MYNSIEM, literally meaning "Dances of Happy Soul," is the dance festival of the Khasis and is held in April/May at Mawlai field, Shillong, as a thanks-giving to the Almighty. Only virgin girts can participate unlike the males who may well be married. The dance costumes are of silk and muslin while the jewellery is of 24 carat gold and silver. The NONGKREM DANCE is held in Syiemship of Smit during September/October, exhibits almost the same dance form and is a popular tourist attraction. The I.AHOO is the traditional dance of the Jaintia people. Originally called the CHI PI AH Dance, the present name has evolved from the "hooh-ah-hooh" chant of the performers. A female danseuse is flanked by two male dancers - the maiden representing the custodian

of the family & preserver of the race. The man on the right symbolises the uncle or the protector of family and clan. Dancing on the left is the husband or father considered as the progenitor of a particular family or clan. The lone maiden, dancing in rhythm, symbolises the priestess : care-taker of family and clan, religious rites & rituals. The WANGALA is performed by the Garos during their 100 Drums Festival of the same name. Celebrated following the harvest season, young men and women, clad in colourful finery, dance to the rhythm of drums, flutes and song. It is said that the young drummers and the maidens find opportunity, during this festival, to know each other - and choose their future life-partners. Forests and Wildlife Forests have always been an integral part of the people of the state. Be it for timber, firewood or other forest produce like broomstick, bay leaf, cinnamon, etc., forests have been the source of sustenance to the ever-increasing need of man. However, the rich biodiversity of primary forests are disappearing as they give way to only secondary scrub forests due to their continual exploitation by the people. Forests under the control of the State Government account for only 4.43 percent of the total geographical area but these are about the only areas where there is some greenery left. The rest of the forests which are clan, community or privately owned have been recklessly exploited for agriculture and commercial purposes. The forest types include the sal forests, the mixed moist deciduous forests, the evergreen forests, bamboo forests, pine forests and grass- lands. Some of the important timber species include the sal, pine, gamari titachap, teak and makrisal. Many rare plants which have become endemic to only certain pockets include the pygmy lily, pitcher plant, sundew, wild citrus, some rare bamboos, canes and a number of varieties of orchids including the lady's slipper orchid. Therer are two national parks in the State : Balphakram National Park and Nokrak National Park. The wildlife sanctuaries include the

Nongkhyllem Wildlife Sanctuary and the Siju Wildlife Sanctuary. These form the habitat for a number of the rare and threatened birds and animals. Some of the birds which are unique to the area include the great pied hornbill, kalij pheasant, emerald dove, red jungle .fowl, peacock pheasant, racket tailed drongo, Himalayan golden back wookpecker, black naped oriole. The checklist of mammals includes the binturong, clouded leopard, flying squirrel, golden cat, hispid hare, hoolock gibbon, gaur, tiger and elephant. The Forest Department in the State has been making a lot of efforts in afforestation of the already barren areas with the help and cooperation of the local populace. For the control of pollution in urban areas, erratic rainfall and climate changes, planting of trees in every vacant space and protection of existing forests with its wildlife has become an immediate necessity. An enlightened community geared up for action is the only answer if we are to save whatever is left of our forests. T.T.C.MARAK, I.F.S. Divisional Forest Officer Khasl Hills Division, Shillong. A land of blue green hills, cascading rapids, carpets of flowers and unwinding rivers. Manipur lies in the eastern most corner of India. Rich with tradition this oval shaped valley is surrounded by an aura of mystery. Legends say that the discovery of Manipur is the result of the delight the gods took in dancing. Polo is said to have originated from Manipur. Sogol Kangjej (Manipur Polo) is the chief sport in the state even today. Sandwiched between Burma in the East and South and Bangladesh in the West, Mizoram occupies an area of great strategic importance in the North-Eastern corner of India. It is generally cool in summer and not very cold in winter. The winter skies are wonderfully blue and in the morning the mist forming between the hills gives an

enchanting view of wide stretches resembling a vast lake. This exquisitely picturesque, vibrantly colourful, lush fertile narrow strip of mountain territory covers an area of 1 6,579 sq.kms. The state consists of seven districts with sixteen tribes and sub-tribes who speak English besides Ao, Konyak, Angami, Serna, Lotha and other tribes who have their own dialects. They are said to belong to the Indo-Mongoloid stock, a race whose presence was first noted 10 centuries before Christ. Sanskrit literature describes them as kiratas or hillmen living on nature's gifts, warlike and possessing formidable weapons. The ceremonial dress of each tribe is quite fascinating; the multi- colour spear, ceremonial dao, bracelets, chest plates and head dress of coloured bamboo. Each tribe is proud of the distinguishing colours and patterns woven in their shawls. The tribes are full of folklore and fond of seasonal songs, solo, duet and choric. The most popular ones eulogise ancestors, warriors and traditional heroes. Kohima, the state capital is a hill station, situated at an altitude of 1,495 metres above sea level. Tripura, a picturesque hilly region is the second smallest state of India. Covering an area of about 10,500 sq. kms., it was a former princely state. Tripura is bounded on the north, west, south and south-east by international boundary of Bangladesh. In the east, it has a common boundary with Mizoram and Assam. The scenic beauty of Tripura, its forests and lakes and above all its flora and fauna are a delight to the sight. Its rich and varied culture, its handloom and handicraft which is exquisite in colour, excellent in design and craftsmanship, are temptation to the visitor. Tripura is inhabited by various ethnic groups with the cultural heritage of one community differing from another. Inspite of the diverse ethnic groups maintaining their distinct cultural identities, they have mingled into a single whole giving birth to a unique cultural genre. Agartala, the capital is surrounded by hills on three sides. The present site of Agartala was chosen by Maharaja Krishna Kishore Manikya Bahadur who shifted the Capital from old Agartala. DUMOOR LAKE — (110 kms.) Deep green islands dot the panorama of transparent waters, Feel the thrill of a motorboat or float aimlessly in a country boat. BHUBHANESWARI TEMPLE — (110 kms.) The temple has been immortalised by Rabindranath Tagore's famous plays Visarjan & Rajarshi. Built by Maharaja Govinda Manikya, the temple is situated on the right bank of the river Gumti at Udaipur. UNAKOTI — (180 kms. from Agartala) Along a serpentine carpeted road is Unakoti Tirtha - a holy place for thousand of pilgrims. Magnificent rock figures and stone images dating to the 12th century are found here. There is also an image of Lord Shiva, holding a conch in the left hand, a position seldom found elsewhere. JUNGLE MAGIC SEPAHIJALA WILDLIFE SANCTUARY — The sanctuary covers an area of 18.53 sq.kms. and has a rich collection of wildlife, particularly birds and primates. There is a zoo, botanical garden, picnic spot and lake. Enjoy an elephant ride or sit in the toy train. To secure labour welfare the Labour Commis- sioner is implementing the rates of minumum wages fixed/revised from time to time for various employ- ments which at present stand at Rs. 25/- per day for unskilled labour and Rs. 30/- per day for skilled labour. There are two Labour Welfare Centres at Sohra

in East Khasi Hills and Mendipathar in East Qaro Hills.. These centres provide elementary training in Sewing, Knitting, and Embroidery and also recrea- tional facilities to workers and their family members. The number of trainees being trained each year is about 50 in both the centres. Issued by the Labour Commissioner, Meghalaya, Shillong. — - — o The Directorate of Employment and Craftsmen Training functions through a net work of Employment Exchanges and Industrial Training Institutes in the State. The Employment Exchanges render employment assis- tance to Job-seekers and provide them with Vocational Guidance and Occupational Information for showing their careers. The Coaching-cum Guidance Centre , Shillong assists the Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes candidates to compete In recruitment conducted by various agencies. The Industrial Training Institutes impart Vocational Training to youths in different trades like Electrician , Motor Mechanic etc. etc. ThelndustrialTraln- ing Institute for Women , Shillong imparts training in the trade of Dress-making. Successful trainees can look for wage-paid Job or go In for self-employment Issued by the Directorate of Employment & Craftsmen Training
